keyVerseText: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb ἀναπαύω (anapaúō) is formed from the prefix ἀνά (aná), meaning 'up' or 'through,' combined with παύω, meaning 'to cease' or 'to stop.' This composition conveys the fundamental idea of causing a cessation or pause, which extends metaphorically to the concepts of resting or refreshing. Beyond the common English gloss of 'rest,' the root sense emphasizes an active intervention that brings about relief or a halt to labor or trouble, highlighting both physical and spiritual reprieve.
usageInScripture: Across its twelve occurrences, ἀναπαύω consistently conveys the idea of rest or refreshment, whether by giving or taking it. The top translations include 'rest,' 'take your rest,' and 'refresh,' reflecting its core meaning of cessation from toil or distress. The word also appears in reflexive forms indicating repose or exemption, and occasionally in agricultural contexts, illustrating a broad but coherent semantic range centered on the theme of relief and cessation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἀναπαύω enriches our grasp of biblical rest as more than mere inactivity; it is a divine provision of relief and renewal. This verb captures the gracious action of God in halting human burdens and refreshing weary souls, a theme deeply woven into the Christian faith. It points to the spiritual rest found in Christ, who invites those burdened to experience true cessation from their labors. Such rest is both a present reality and a future hope, reflecting God's care and the believer's reliance on His sustaining grace.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 11:28, Jesus invites all who labor and are heavy laden to 'come unto me' for rest. The use of ἀναπαύω here underscores that this rest is a divine gift—an active cessation from weariness and burden provided by Christ himself. This rest is not merely physical but deeply spiritual, offering refreshment and relief that only He can give. The word highlights the personal and relational aspect of this rest, emphasizing that it is found in coming to Jesus and trusting in His sustaining power.
